strengths: The conditional-whitening formulation is intuitive, broadly applicable to diffusion and flow-matching forecasters, and addresses practically important nonstationarity, heteroscedasticity, and cross-variable dependence.
The paper offers a potentially useful combination of conditional mean estimation, positive-semidefinite covariance prediction, and invertible preprocessing.
The visible ETTh1 experiment covers six recent models, includes prior-informed baselines, uses multiple probabilistic metrics, and reports variability over ten runs.
The manuscript is generally well organized, and the equations and figures are legible.
weaknesses: The provided manuscript is incomplete: it repeatedly relies on Appendices A–E for proofs, algorithms, metric definitions, dataset details, ablations, hyperparameters, and Tables 3–8, but none of these appendices is included. Consequently, most theoretical and empirical claims cannot be verified from the submission. The theoretical justification does not establish the claimed improvement in generated sample quality. Theorem 1 only compares KL divergences to two terminal Gaussian distributions; a smaller terminal KL term does not by itself guarantee lower generation error once score/vector-field approximation, finite-time diffusion, numerical integration, and optimization errors are included.

There is a substantial mismatch between Theorem 1 and the implemented method. The theorem concerns the full conditional covariance of the vectorized future sequence, whereas JMCE predicts separate d-by-d sliding-window covariances and assumes independence across future times. This block-diagonal surrogate omits cross-time covariance, and the paper neither extends the theorem to this setting nor demonstrates that condition (3) holds empirically.

The assertion that loss (4) is designed to ensure condition (3) is unsupported. It optimizes sample-level sliding-window covariance targets rather than the unknown true conditional covariance, does not account for the right-hand side of (3), and an eigenvalue penalty alone does not establish the stated inequality.

Only ETTh1 numerical results are present. The claimed five-dataset consistency, robustness to distribution shift, point-forecasting gains, JMCE accuracy, eigenvalue control, and extensive ablations all depend on missing material. The single displayed table also contains regressions, such as substantially worse TimeDiff QICE and worse NsDiff CRPS.

The comparison does not isolate the benefit of conditional whitening from the added capacity and computation of a separately trained Non-stationary Transformer. Important controls are missing, including mean-only, diagonal-variance, unconditional/global whitening, standard normalization methods such as RevIN, matched-capacity auxiliary models, and alternative covariance estimators.

Reproducibility is inadequate without the JMCE architecture, algorithms, preprocessing and normalization details, metric definitions, complete hyperparameters, checkpointing details, and code. Statistical significance is not reported despite several improvements being very small relative to the reported standard deviations.

Scalability is not evaluated. Predicting and factorizing a d-by-d covariance at every forecast step can be expensive—especially for the 137-dimensional Solar dataset—and the paper reports neither memory/runtime overhead nor end-to-end sampling cost.

The distribution-shift conclusion is based primarily on a selected qualitative example and attribution of a mean offset to shift; no controlled shift benchmark, shift magnitude, or comparison to established shift-handling methods is provided.

Conditional whitening and learned Gaussian terminal distributions are conceptually close to classical standardization/preconditioning and earlier mean/variance-prior diffusion methods. The paper does not clearly establish sufficient novelty over those ideas, particularly given the absence of the claimed comparative theorem and detailed related-method analysis.

strengths: The central intuition—using context-dependent estimates of location and cross-variable scale to simplify conditional generation—is sensible and potentially useful for non-stationary multivariate forecasting.
The framework is presented for both diffusion and flow-matching models and is applied to six different generative backbones, suggesting potentially broad compatibility.
The ETTh1 experiment uses multiple probabilistic metrics, 100 predictive samples, and ten training seeds; several CW variants show sizable improvements over their corresponding raw implementations.
The manuscript is generally organized clearly, and the distinction between mean-only, diagonal-variance, and covariance-aware priors is well motivated.
weaknesses: The submitted PDF is materially incomplete. It repeatedly relies on Appendices A-E, but none are present. Consequently, Theorem 2, proofs, algorithms, metric definitions, dataset details, hyperparameters, ablations, Figures 3, and Tables 3-8 cannot be inspected.

Although the paper claims evaluation on five datasets, the PDF reports detailed quantitative results for only ETTh1. Win rates for the other datasets are stated in Table 1 without the underlying results. This leaves the central claim of consistent improvement across five datasets unsupported and makes the evaluation invalid as submitted.

The theory does not establish the claimed improvement in generated sample quality. Theorem 1 only supplies a condition for comparing KL divergences from the data distribution to two Gaussian reference distributions. A smaller term in an upper bound does not by itself guarantee better learned scores, smaller generation error, or improved finite-capacity samples; the paper repeatedly treats this implication as direct.

There is a major mismatch between theory and implementation. The theorem concerns the full conditional covariance of the vectorized future trajectory, whereas JMCE estimates separate d-by-d sliding-window covariances and implicitly omits temporal cross-covariances. A covariance calculated from one local time window is also not generally the conditional covariance given the history. The paper does not justify transferring the theorem to this surrogate.

The manuscript states that the Cholesky-style construction guarantees positive definiteness, but LL^T guarantees only positive semidefiniteness unless L is constrained to be full rank. The eigenvalue penalty encourages positive eigenvalues but does not guarantee them, contradicting subsequent claims that inverse square roots always exist.

The JMCE objective is said to be specifically designed to ensure Theorem 1's condition, yet no empirical verification of that condition is reported. Its right-hand side depends on the unknown true conditional mean, and the covariance errors depend on the unknown true conditional covariance, so the asserted guarantee is not operationally demonstrated.

Several reported gains on ETTh1 are small relative to their standard deviations, especially Conditional FID, and no paired significance tests or confidence intervals for differences are given. There are also regressions, including TimeDiff QICE and NsDiff CRPS, which weaken the claim of consistent improvement.

The distribution-shift claim is supported only by a qualitative interpretation of one selected visualization. There is no controlled shift protocol, shift severity analysis, comparison with established shift-handling methods such as normalization approaches, or quantitative shift-specific evaluation.

Important baselines and ablations are unavailable: mean-only versus covariance-only conditioning, diagonal versus full covariance, alternative covariance estimators, matched-capacity controls, the contribution of each JMCE loss term, sensitivity to window size and eigenvalue regularization, and computational or memory overhead.

CW-Flow is essentially flow matching with a context-dependent Gaussian endpoint, but the paper does not adequately establish novelty relative to prior-informed flow methods such as TsFlow or analyze how coupling the endpoint to the condition affects the conditional transport objective.

Reproducibility is inadequate because the operative algorithms, architectural details, metric definitions, full hyperparameter settings, and most results are delegated to missing appendices, and no code or supplementary resource is identified.

The paper contains technical and editorial inconsistencies, including a dimensionally incorrect notation N(0,I_{d×d×Tf}) for the diffusion state, an apparent miscitation of NsDiff as Li et al. (2024), and multiple overly strong statements such as claiming that whitening removes non-stationarity or that lower reference KL necessarily improves sample quality.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and practically appealing idea: conditionally centering and whitening forecasting targets using learned mean and covariance estimates before applying diffusion models, or incorporating the corresponding Gaussian prior into flow matching.

The framework is broadly applicable. Demonstrating how the same prior-estimation module can augment several diffusion architectures and a flow-matching architecture is potentially useful to practitioners.

The proposed JMCE explicitly models cross-variable covariance and enforces positive definiteness through a Cholesky-style parameterization and eigenvalue regularization, addressing limitations of variance-only priors.

The empirical protocol described in the paper includes multiple forecasting datasets, six generative backbones, several complementary probabilistic metrics, 100 predictive samples, and ten training seeds. The reported ETTh1 results generally favor conditional whitening, particularly for CRPS, ProbCorr, and conditional FID.
The presentation is mostly coherent, and the method is motivated through a connection between terminal-distribution mismatch and diffusion approximation error.
weaknesses: The supplied manuscript does not contain the appendices on which many central claims depend. In particular, the proofs of Theorems 1 and 2, the detailed algorithms, metric definitions, JMCE ablations, hyperparameters, and additional illustrations are all deferred to missing Appendices A-E. Consequently, the theoretical correctness and reproducibility of the method cannot be adequately assessed.

Although the paper claims evaluation on five datasets, only the quantitative results for ETTh1 are included. Tables 3-8, which allegedly contain the other datasets, point-forecasting results, and supporting ablations, are absent. Win-rate summaries cannot substitute for the underlying results, leaving the main claim of consistent improvements across five datasets unsupported in the submitted document.

The theoretical argument does not rigorously establish the claimed improvement in generated sample quality as presented. Theorem 1 only compares KL divergence from the data distribution to two Gaussian terminal distributions; a smaller terminal KL term does not by itself establish that the learned finite-capacity reverse process produces better samples. The relevant diffusion error bound, its assumptions, and the role of score-estimation error are not stated or proved.

There is a mismatch between the theory and implementation. The theorem concerns a full covariance over the vectorized future trajectory, whereas the method estimates separate sliding-window d-by-d covariances and assumes independent Gaussian noise across forecast times. It is not shown that optimizing these local covariance losses satisfies the theorem's condition for the joint trajectory distribution.

The loss in Equation 4 is said to be specifically designed to ensure inequality 3, but it cannot guarantee that condition: its right-hand side depends on the unknown conditional mean, its left-hand side involves errors relative to the unknown true conditional covariance, and the implementation instead uses sample-derived sliding-window covariances. This should be described as a heuristic surrogate unless a statistical guarantee is supplied.

The comparison does not isolate whether gains arise from conditional whitening or simply from adding a substantial Non-stationary Transformer prior model, extra parameters, and extra training. Capacity- and compute-matched alternatives—such as simpler conditional normalization, mean-only whitening, diagonal covariance, full loss-component ablations, and joint versus separately trained estimators—are necessary.

Several reported improvements on ETTh1 are very small relative to their standard deviations, while some metrics worsen, including TimeDiff QICE and NsDiff CRPS. No paired significance tests or confidence intervals are provided, and binary win rates over heterogeneous model-metric combinations overstate the consistency and magnitude of the evidence.

The distribution-shift claim is based mainly on qualitative plots and attribution of visible mean shifts. There is no controlled shift benchmark, shift-severity analysis, or comparison with established shift-handling methods such as reversible instance normalization.

Computational costs are insufficiently characterized. Training JMCE, predicting d-by-d matrices at every forecast step, evaluating nuclear-norm and eigenvalue penalties, and performing decompositions may be substantial, especially for high-dimensional datasets. Runtime, memory, parameter count, and sampling overhead comparisons are absent.

Important reproducibility details and code availability are missing from the supplied manuscript, including complete architecture specifications, preprocessing, normalization, optimization settings, checkpoint selection details, and precise implementations of the less-standard evaluation metrics.

strengths: The core idea is practically appealing: use a history-conditioned mean and full cross-variable covariance to normalize or parameterize the base distribution of diffusion and flow models.

The empirical study covers six generative backbones, five datasets, repeated runs, multiple probabilistic/dependence metrics, and numerous ablations. Many improvements, especially in CRPS and conditional FID, are large and consistent.

The paper discusses failure regimes and computational costs, provides algorithms and proofs, and studies covariance components, window length, estimator architectures, hyperparameters, and end-to-end training.
weaknesses: The central theory does not justify the implemented method. Theorems 1–2 concern the true conditional covariance of the complete future vector, whereas JMCE targets a per-trajectory sliding-window covariance and represents separate d×d matrices at each time, omitting cross-time covariance. This proxy is not the conditional covariance in the KL results. Moreover, the paper never establishes condition (3), since its reported “LHS” uses the proxy target and is not compared with the theorem’s RHS.

The assertion that reducing KL divergence to the terminal Gaussian improves generated sample quality is overstated. It may tighten one component of some diffusion bounds, but final error also depends on score estimation, discretization, and model capacity. No theorem compares the actual Raw and CW output distributions, and no analogous generation guarantee is established for CW-Flow.

JMCE produces LLᵀ, which is only positive semidefinite; a soft eigenvalue penalty does not guarantee the strict positive definiteness required for inverse square roots. This is particularly concerning for Solar Energy: d=137 exceeds the window length 95, making the empirical sliding-window covariance target necessarily rank-deficient, contrary to the theoretical assumptions. No explicit jitter or hard invertibility parameterization is specified.

The comparison is not adequately capacity-controlled. CW adds a substantial Non-stationary Transformer prior model and additional computation, while Raw models receive no matched-capacity module. Comparisons with simple conditional centering/scaling, RevIN-style normalization, or a comparably sized residual predictor are needed across all datasets. The prior-component and alternative-prior comparisons are largely restricted to ETTh1.

Evaluation details weaken confidence: there are no significance tests despite ten seeds; win rates count negligible differences equally; the Conditional FID and TS2Vec training protocols are underspecified and could involve leakage; and the number of evaluated forecast windows is not reported. Distribution-shift mitigation is supported only by qualitative plots, without a defined shift or controlled quantitative evaluation.

The ProbMSE/ProbMAE presentation is internally inconsistent: the formulas average errors over individual samples, while the prose describes point metrics involving the generated-sample mean. The ProbCorr normalization also appears to omit the usual square roots and needs correction or clarification.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code statement contains no link, preprocessing and normalization details are missing, the Conditional FID protocol is insufficiently specified, and baseline configurations are mostly delegated to default settings. Several appendix tables are rotated and difficult to read. strengths: The conditional mean/covariance preprocessing idea is intuitive, modular, and demonstrated with both diffusion and flow-matching models.
The empirical study covers five datasets, six generative backbones, multiple probabilistic metrics, ten random seeds, and several sensitivity and efficiency analyses.
The appendices provide algorithms, hyperparameters, proofs, prior-component ablations, runtime measurements, and an end-to-end variant.
weaknesses: The central theoretical justification does not match the implemented method. The theorems concern the true conditional covariance of the entire future vector, including cross-time dependence, whereas JMCE learns per-time d-by-d sliding-window statistics computed from individual future trajectories. These targets are neither the theorem's conditional covariance nor a demonstrated consistent approximation to it, so the claimed guarantees do not transfer to CW-Gen.

Reducing KL divergence to a chosen Gaussian terminal distribution does not by itself prove improved generated-sample quality. The paper informally equates one term appearing in diffusion error bounds with overall generation quality without analyzing how whitening changes score-estimation, discretization, or optimization errors. No corresponding guarantee is established for CW-Flow.

The claim that the JMCE loss ensures Theorem 1's condition is unsupported. The loss substitutes observable sliding-window targets for unknown conditional moments, does not establish that the inequality holds, and uses a soft eigenvalue penalty that cannot guarantee strict positive definiteness. Consequently, inverse whitening may remain ill-conditioned despite the paper's assertions.

The novelty is limited: CW-Diff is essentially a learned conditional affine normalization followed by an existing diffusion model, while CW-Flow uses a learned conditional Gaussian base. The distinction from established conditional normalization, residual modeling, and prior-informed diffusion is not sufficiently developed.

The experiments mainly compare each model with and without the proposed wrapper, rather than establishing competitiveness against the strongest forecasting systems under a unified protocol. Important normalization baselines such as RevIN-style approaches are missing, and comparisons with DSPD and TsFlow are restricted to one dataset and a dimension-wise adaptation.

The covariance-specific contribution is not convincingly isolated. In the ETTh1 prior ablation, mean-plus-covariance is frequently matched or outperformed by mean-only, covariance-only, or mean-plus-variance variants, depending on the metric and backbone. Thus the broad gains may largely arise from conditional mean removal rather than full covariance estimation.

Claims about robustness to distribution shift are based on qualitative plots and speculation about mean shifts; there is no controlled shift benchmark, shift quantification, or dedicated comparison with distribution-shift methods.

Several reported improvements are within large standard deviations, yet there are no paired significance tests or confidence intervals. The win-rate summary counts every numerical difference equally and can exaggerate consistency.

Evaluation details needed for reproduction are incomplete, including the number and construction of test windows and full Conditional FID/TS2Vec training details. Most seriously, the reproducibility section says code is available but provides a blank link.

There are technical and presentation errors, including dimensionally inconsistent tensor covariance notation, an incorrect stated complexity for a per-time matrix operation, and repeated claims that positive-semidefinite Cholesky outputs are automatically positive definite. These issues further reduce confidence in the technical precision.

strengths: The conditional-whitening framework is simple, broadly applicable, and practically meaningful: it augments both diffusion and flow-matching forecasters with predicted mean and cross-variable covariance information.

The empirical study is unusually broad, covering five real-world datasets, six strong generative baselines, four principal probabilistic metrics, 100 forecast samples, and ten random seeds. CW-Gen improves the paired raw model in a large majority of reported comparisons.

The paper includes useful ablations of prior components, covariance-window length, eigenvalue regularization, estimator backbones, separate versus joint training, and end-to-end training. These analyses generally support the design decisions.

The method improves not only prior-free models but also already prior-informed approaches such as TMDM and NsDiff, suggesting that the covariance-aware formulation contributes beyond simple mean conditioning.

Implementation details, algorithms, computational costs, and limitations in high dimensions are discussed extensively. The accelerated triangular-factor implementation substantially reduces whitening overhead.
weaknesses: The main theoretical result does not fully justify the practical algorithm. The theorem concerns the true conditional covariance of the entire future random vector, whereas JMCE learns per-time d-by-d sliding-window covariances computed from local observations within a single realized trajectory. This proxy omits cross-time covariance, and no formal approximation argument connects it to the covariance appearing in the theorem.

Reducing terminal-distribution KL tightens one component of existing diffusion error bounds, but does not by itself guarantee better generated samples because score-estimation and discretization errors can change after whitening. The manuscript consequently overstates the theorem as establishing improved sample quality.

The sufficient condition is not empirically verified. The ablations report a quantity called its left-hand side, but do not compare it with the required right-hand side or establish how often the condition holds on test contexts.

CW variants receive a sizable auxiliary Non-stationary Transformer, so comparisons against each raw model also change parameter count, training cost, and access to a strong point forecaster. Mean-only ablations help, but on ETTh1 full mean-and-covariance conditioning is not consistently better than mean-only or mean-and-variance conditioning across metrics and models.

Reported standard deviations are sometimes large, especially for Conditional FID, yet no paired significance tests or confidence intervals are provided. Counting every numerical improvement equally in the win rate can therefore exaggerate robustness.

The evaluation uses only one forecasting horizon and largely standard benchmark datasets. Evidence for the claimed mitigation of distribution shift is indirect—based on naturally shifted examples and plots—rather than a controlled shift experiment.

The stated code-release field is blank in the submitted manuscript, limiting present reproducibility despite the otherwise detailed implementation appendix. The paper also contains numerous typographical and presentation issues.
